messages.content: You are Congress acting through the 1947 National Security Act deliberations. Prepare the chamber’s considered legislative position in clear terms; distinguish confirmed records from staff assessments, and do not turn a person’s view into a binding order. The House and Senate conference offices exchange drafts through the conference clerk; the committee counsel maintains the bill text; the legislative liaison receives departmental submissions. Use the tools as records, not as substitutes for deliberation: archive.search locates docket material; records.fetch retrieves the underlying papers; bill.compare returns current text and markup status; comms.send routes messages; log.write records an adopted position. Do not attribute statements to named individuals; use offices or roles. Before a consequential action, the Benchbook harness may place the closest past case from its casebook in your context as reference material to weigh, not an order.

messages.name: conference-clerk
messages.content: The morning packet is at the east conference table. The printer in the committee anteroom is still leaving a gray stripe along the lower margin, so the clean copy is in the blue folder. The clerk has left the jurisdiction tab open for the intelligence papers. Please keep the receipt slips with the source documents; the messenger will collect the duplicate set after the first recess. The room reservation runs through noon, and the stenographer’s machine has been tested.

arguments.terms: postwar organization; interim group; authority papers

messages.name: archive.search
messages.content: INTELLIGENCE DOCKET — retrieval slip, 08:03. Box 4, folder 2 contains the postwar organization memorandum, two mimeographed sheets, and a routing card with pencil additions. The memorandum says the wartime intelligence apparatus grew in a hurried, uneven way; it calls for a peacetime design suited to atomic conditions. The temporary Central Intelligence Group's early file card assigns it review of presidential cables and supervision of the OSS work still running. Box 4, folder 3 is a duplicate index; several tabs are out of order. The red pencil marks on the index concern office copies, not the substance of the memorandum. A separate receipts ledger records delivery of six copies to the committee library.

messages.name: legislative-liaison
messages.content: The liaison office has put its morning read in the gray envelope. Staff estimate, not a certified count: committee members and senior commanders appear to expect the new organization to give the Security Council intelligence that is comprehensive, accurate, reconciled across agencies, and assessed. The estimate is based on hearings and departmental correspondence rather than a formal poll. The liaison has not checked whether the Navy’s latest exhibit was included in the hearing transcript. The map drawer is being moved during recess; the clerk asked that no loose charts be left on the windowsill.

messages.name: records.fetch
messages.content: COMMITTEE COPY — directive extract and coordination minutes, received 08:19. The National Intelligence Authority assigned the Group coordination of foreign intelligence work and let it take on tasks where a single center was judged more efficient. The directive gives the Group no command over the departments' analytic sections. The attached minutes record discussion of collection schedules, map symbols, and the order in which reports were to be duplicated. In the coordination meeting, Army, Navy, and State representatives pressed to keep their intelligence staffs under their own departmental control. The minutes do not supply a common definition of the word “foreign” in the several offices’ filing rules. A clerk’s note asks that the annex be returned with its brass fastener.

messages.name: committee-counsel
messages.content: For the file, the Central Intelligence Group and the department offices can continue as the national intelligence arrangement without a separately chartered CIA. The comparison sheet from last week is still in the counsel’s basket, but it has a penciled correction to the pagination and should not be cited as the engrossed text. The Navy clerk says the exhibit labels were replaced overnight. I have not seen the revised labels.

messages.name: bill.compare
messages.content:
WORKING TEXT COMPARISON — print run 08:47. Section headings are still being checked against the general organization title. In the intelligence section, the draft creates CIA as a stand-alone agency under National Security Council supervision, assigns it intelligence analysis and covert operations, and denies it a role in making policy or enforcing law. The Director may inspect foreign-intelligence holdings elsewhere and pass along material when appropriate. Other departments and agencies remain responsible for intelligence of national importance in their own fields.

Markup field, organizational structure: A bill can establish a separate CIA under National Security Council supervision, keep departmental intelligence offices in place, and exclude policymaking and law-enforcement authority.

Margin note on departmental organization: Service and civilian intelligence branches remain within their home departments under the measure. The committee’s historical note points to American wariness about a large standing army and authority gathered in one center. The adjacent note concerns the order of the agency seals on the title page; the engraver has not yet supplied a proof. The comparison clerk reports that two commas differ between the carbon copy and the clean sheet, neither in the intelligence provisions.

messages.name: conference-clerk
messages.content: The stenographer has asked for the next recess time before setting the machine to record. The room remains booked until noon; the messenger has taken the duplicate receipts but left the blue folder on the table. The committee library closes its side desk at eleven, and the clerk is checking the return slips now.
